transcript.text: Samsung WD90T534DBW washer dryer - clothes are still damp at the end of the wash and dry programme. It's not that old. Is the heater going?

Not necessarily. Damp clothes at the end of a wash-and-dry programme are more often caused by too much in the dry load, a low/short drying setting, or the clothes going into drying insufficiently spun. A heater fault becomes more likely only if there is no warmth at all during the drying stage. 1. Check the load and programme: a washer-dryer can dry substantially less than it can wash, so a full wash load commonly finishes damp. Try a smaller load on a full drying programme/high dryness setting. If that cures it, there is no heater fault. 2. Check whether it gets warm: during a drying cycle, carefully open the door only when the machine permits it, or feel the laundry immediately afterwards. Warm but damp points to the condensing/airflow or water-removal side, rather than the heater. Completely cold points towards the drying heater, thermostat or thermal cut-out. 3. Make sure the cold-water tap is fully on and the inlet and drain hoses behind the machine are not kinked. Washer-dryers commonly use cold water to condense moisture during drying and then pump that water away; a restricted supply or drain can leave laundry damp. 4. If accessible, switch off and unplug first, put towels and a shallow tray down, then clean the pump/drain filter behind the lower front flap. Fluff or debris there can restrict removal of condensed water. During the drying part, does the drum/clothing become noticeably warm, and was the load no more than the machine's stated dry capacity (not its larger wash capacity)?
Yes, the drum gets hot during drying and the clothes are hot but damp at the end. The load is a full 9kg drum, washed and dried in one go, and the manual says 6kg dry capacity.

No — the heater is very unlikely to be the problem. The drum and clothes becoming hot shows it is producing heat. The 9 kg figure is the wash capacity, whereas the 6 kg figure is the maximum it can dry. Putting the full 9 kg straight into drying leaves too little space for warm air and moisture removal, so hot-but-damp laundry is the expected result rather than evidence of a fault. 1. Split the load: dry no more than 6 kg at a time — slightly less is often better for towels, jeans or thick cottons.
2. Use a full drying programme or the higher dryness setting, rather than a short timed dry.
3. Keep the cold-water tap fully open and check the drain hose is not squashed; the machine needs to remove condensed moisture during drying. If a load within the 6 kg limit still comes out hot and distinctly damp after a full dry programme, then clean the pump/drain filter (unplug first, with towels and a shallow tray ready). If that is clear and the problem persists, the likely issue is on the condensation/airflow or water-removal side and an engineer would be sensible — but not the heater as the first suspect.

candidates: Dry load too large, short/low drying setting, or clothes entering drying too wet (high)
Restricted condensing/drain path or water supply during drying (medium)
Drying heater, thermostat or thermal cut-out fault (low)
